897.title: The Karorsinghia misl
897.hook: a misl of the Doaba lands
897.howItsDone: Sikh histories describe each misl by its leaders and its home country; families in Punjab sometimes still remember which misl their village rode with.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Singhpuria misl, Nawab Kapur Singh's own riders. Your line was the nawab's band. Who did you hand the credit to? Today, a band that belonged to a stretch of land. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

Wedding drums in one village, and the next village over can hear them. Wheat, sugarcane, mango groves, flat green farmland between the Beas and the Sutlej. Punjabis call it the Doaba. A family there knows the families in the villages around it, and whose grandfather dug which well. In the misl years, riders from those villages saddled up together and fought as one band. Their neighbors knew them by their leader's name, and the land knew them as its own. Today: the Karorsinghia misl.
screen: `WEDDING DRUMS ACROSS THE FIELDS.` → `THE DOABA, BETWEEN THE BEAS AND THE SUTLEJ.` → `A BAND FROM ITS VILLAGES.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Sikh histories say this misl was called after one of its leaders, Karora Singh. So the name carries a person. But the band itself belonged to a place. Its riders came largely from the Doaba, the land between the two rivers, and that is where their strength sat. Here's why that matters. A misl was not an army on a map. It was farmers' sons, cousins, neighbors, men who knew which well was sweet and whose field bordered whose. When they rode, they rode for a village they could name. When danger passed, they went home to it. The second turn of the story is a later leader, Baghel Singh. Tradition says he took this band far beyond the Doaba, all the way to Delhi. And the story Sikhs tell about him is not mainly about conquest. Tradition says that while he was there, he sought out the places in the city tied to the Gurus, and saw that they were marked. Gurdwaras stand at such places in Delhi today, and Sikh memory links some of them to his search. So a band rooted in one patch of farmland reached a far city, and what it is remembered for there is remembering. The third turn is the plainest. A misl's home ground shaped it. A band of the Doaba knew its fields, its wells and its neighbors' families, and it carried that knowledge into its fights and its peace. Faith was the same faith in every band. Place gave each one its own accent.

The sound outside your window early in the morning. The road you take without thinking. Notice one way that place has shaped you, the way you talk, what you eat, what you expect from strangers. You don't have to like it. Just notice it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

898.title: The Shaheedan misl
898.hook: the martyrs' misl, linked to Baba Deep Singh
898.howItsDone: In Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh services, Sikhs remember the martyrs who held to their faith; Baba Deep Singh is remembered at gurdwaras in Amritsar and at Damdama Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Karorsinghia misl, riders from the farmland between two rivers. Your line was a band of the doaba. What did you notice about your own ground? Today, a band named not for a place or a leader. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

The misls you've met this block mostly wear a name you could find on a map, or on a family tree. A village. A leader. A stretch of country. The Nishanwalias took theirs from a duty. Today's band chose something else again. It called itself after the dead. Not after a defeat, and not after a grief, exactly. After the people who had given their lives and whose example the riders meant to keep. Shaheed is the Punjabi word for a martyr. Today: the Shaheedan misl, the band of the martyrs.
screen: `A VILLAGE, A LEADER, A COUNTRY, A DUTY.` → `ONE BAND CHOSE THE DEAD.` → `SHAHEED: A MARTYR.`

segments.voice: Sikh tradition ties this band to Baba Deep Singh. This path has already told his story: the old scholar who left his study at Damdama Sahib to defend the Harmandir, and who, tradition says, fought on to reach the holy precinct even after a mortal wound. The Shaheedan misl is remembered as the band that grew from those around him, and that kept his name and his place alive afterward. So here's the first thing a name does. It tells the riders who they are before anyone gives an order. A band called after a village rides for that village. A band called after martyrs rides with them, in a sense. Every time someone said the name, the dead were in the room. The second thing is where the band kept its center. Tradition links it to Damdama Sahib, the place of study where Baba Deep Singh had worked with the scripture. That's a quiet detail and a telling one. A band named for those who died for the faith kept close to the place where the faith was copied, read, and taught. Sword and book in the same hands, a pairing Sikh tradition holds dear. The third thing is the hardest. A name like this could become a boast. Sikh memory doesn't treat martyrdom as a prize to chase. In the daily prayer called Ardas, Sikhs remember those who gave their heads and did not give up their faith, and they ask for the same steadiness, not for a death. The martyrs are remembered so that the living can stand straight. That's the weight a band carried when it called itself the martyrs' band.

899.title: The Phulkian states
899.hook: Patiala, Nabha and Jind, often counted apart from the twelve
899.howItsDone: Sikh histories tell the story of Phul and Guru Har Rai's blessing, and gurdwaras in the former Phulkian lands, such as those in Patiala, are part of Sikh life in the Malwa region today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shaheedan misl, the band named for those who gave their lives. Your line was the martyrs' band. Whose name did you say out loud? Today, a family of chiefs who stood a little to one side. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

A hungry boy is brought before Guru Har Rai. Sikh tradition tells it simply: an uncle brings two small brothers to the Guru, and one of them pats his own empty stomach. The Guru looks at the child and blesses him: his house will grow, and it will feed many. The boy's name was Phul. Generations later, the families who traced their line to him ruled three states south of the Sutlej: Patiala, Nabha and Jind. Today: the Phulkian states.
screen: `A HUNGRY BOY BEFORE GURU HAR RAI.` → `A BLESSING ON HIS HOUSE.` → `PATIALA, NABHA AND JIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the puzzle the Phulkian states set for anyone who counts the misls. Some lists of the twelve misls include them. Others set them apart. Both habits have reasons. The first reason for setting them apart is the river. The Phulkian chiefs held the Malwa country, south of the Sutlej, and that was their whole world. Different neighbors, different dangers, different deals. The second reason is how they ruled. A misl, as this block has described it, was a band of equals around a chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa. The Phulkian houses grew more like ruling families: the leadership passing down a line, the chief becoming a raja. Patiala's founder, Ala Singh, is remembered for building a state, and for making terms with the powers around him at times when other bands were fighting them. Sikh histories judge those terms in more than one way. Some call them shrewd survival. Some call them a step away from the Dal Khalsa. So why are they in this block at all? Because the story starts with the Guru's blessing. The Phulkian families traced their rise to that hungry boy and that hand on his head, and they built and supported gurdwaras across their lands. They stood apart in politics, and they stayed inside the same faith, the same scripture, the same Guru's house. A family can live in a different town and still sit at the same table on the big days. Apart, yet related.

900.title: Twice a year at Amritsar
900.hook: the misls met as the Sarbat Khalsa at Vaisakhi and Diwali to decide together before the Granth
900.howItsDone: Sikhs still speak of the Sarbat Khalsa and the gurmata, and Sikh congregations take decisions before the Guru Granth Sahib, often ending with Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Phulkian states: Patiala, Nabha and Jind, south of the river, sometimes counted with the misls and sometimes not. Your line was apart, yet related. Who did you reach out to? Today, the days when everyone came together. Day nine hundred.

Who decides, when nobody is king? The misl chiefs argued over villages and grazing and who owed whom. Some of them had fought each other. No ruler stood over them to settle it, and each answered to his own riders. Yet at Vaisakhi in spring and Diwali in autumn, Sikh histories say, they came to Amritsar, sat down together, and put the Guru Granth Sahib in front of them. Today: twice a year at Amritsar.
screen: `NOBODY IS KING.` → `RIVALS, EACH WITH HIS OWN RIDERS.` → `ONE PLACE, TWICE A YEAR.`

segments.voice: The gathering had a name: the Sarbat Khalsa. Sarbat means all, the whole. So it was the whole Khalsa, not one chief's council, not a king's court. That's the first thing to notice. In principle, every band had a place in it. The second thing is where they sat. Tradition says the assembly met before the Guru Granth Sahib, near the Akal Takht. The scripture was not a decoration on the wall. It was the presence they were deciding in front of. And that changed the tone of the room. A chief who might shout in his own camp had to speak, here, as one Sikh among others before the Guru. The third thing is what came out of it. A decision reached this way was called a gurmata. Sikhs describe it as a resolution of the Guru, made by the gathered Khalsa in the Guru's presence. Once it was agreed, the bands were bound by it together. Sikh histories say this is how the misls chose shared leaders, planned joint campaigns, and set their quarrels aside, at least for a season. And notice the season. Vaisakhi and Diwali were already festival days, days for coming to Amritsar anyway. The meeting rode on the back of the celebration. People came to bathe in the pool and to see the Harmandir, and while they were there, they decided things. Faith first, then business, and the business done in faith's presence. A people with no single ruler found a way to have a single voice, twice a year. Decide before the Guru.

901.title: The bungas
901.hook: the misls built rest-houses round the sacred pool for pilgrims and defenders
901.howItsDone: Pilgrims to the Harmandir Sahib today stay in the guest houses (sarais) of the complex, free of charge, and some old bunga buildings still stand near the pool.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twice a year at Amritsar: the whole Khalsa gathered at Vaisakhi and Diwali to agree a gurmata before the Guru Granth Sahib. Your line was decide before the guru. Which decision did you slow down? Today, where all those riders slept. Day nine hundred one.

A blanket unrolled on a brick floor, a few steps from the water. A horse tied up outside. A rider who has come a long way leaves his things in a room with thick walls and goes down to bathe in the pool and bow at the Harmandir. That room isn't an inn. Sikh histories say the misls built such houses. Around the sacred pool, one by one, they rose, each put up by a chief or a band. Today's word is what those houses were called: bunga.
screen: `A BLANKET ON A BRICK FLOOR.` → `A FEW STEPS FROM THE WATER.` → `HOUSES RISE AROUND THE POOL.`

segments.voice: A bunga did three jobs at once. The first was rest. Pilgrims coming to the Harmandir needed somewhere to stay, and a bunga gave them a place by the pool: close enough to hear the kirtan, the sung scripture. The guest didn't have to find an inn or bargain for a room. The house was already there, built for exactly this. The second job was defense. These were years when the Harmandir had been attacked and damaged, as this path has told. So a bunga was not a light little guesthouse. Tradition describes them as strong buildings, some with high walls, where defenders could stay and keep watch over the pool and the shrine. Rest and guard duty under the same roof. The third job was a quiet one: belonging. Each bunga was tied to a misl, a chief, or a community, so when riders from that band arrived, they knew where their place was. Their bunga. A misl that might be miles away the rest of the year had a doorway on the edge of the sacred pool. And one building connected to this story is worth naming. Some histories call the building of the Akal Takht itself the Akal Bunga. Whatever the label, it sits facing the Harmandir across the causeway. Over the years the precinct around the pool has been rebuilt, and most of the old bungas have gone, though a few still stand. But the idea is worth keeping: around the Harmandir, the people built rooms for strangers to rest in. Rest by the pool.

902.title: The Ramgarhia towers
902.hook: two tall towers built to guard the Harmandir still stand
902.howItsDone: Pilgrims at the Harmandir Sahib complex in Amritsar can see the towers of the Ramgarhia Bunga near the edge of the precinct, and Sikh histories remember Jassa Singh Ramgarhia as their builder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bungas: houses round the sacred pool where pilgrims slept and defenders kept watch. Your line was rest by the pool. Who did you offer a place to rest? Today, the bunga that grew upward. Day nine hundred two.

Stand on the marble walkway around the pool at the Harmandir and look up and away from the golden shrine, and two brick towers rise above the rooftops near the edge of the complex. They don't glitter. They aren't covered in gold. They look like what they were: lookouts. Sikh tradition says they belong to the bunga of Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, the carpenter's son this block met earlier. Rest-houses once ringed the pool; this one still stands for people to point to. Today: the Ramgarhia towers.
screen: `TWO BRICK TOWERS ABOVE THE ROOFS.` → `NOT GOLD: LOOKOUTS.` → `JASSA SINGH RAMGARHIA'S BUNGA.`

segments.voice: Start with what a tower is for. A wall keeps people out. A tower lets you see them coming. In years when, as this path has told, armies came to Amritsar more than once, the people who loved the Harmandir needed early warning. From the top of a tower, a watchman could see the roads and fields beyond the city long before anyone at the pool could. So the towers are about attention. Somebody climbs up, and stays up, and looks, while others below bathe and pray and sleep. Guarding, in this picture, is mostly patience. Hours of nothing, for the one moment that matters. Now notice who built them. Jassa Singh Ramgarhia came, tradition says, from a carpenter's family, a family of builders. His band's gift to the Harmandir was not mainly gold or a donation. It was a building, made to protect someone else's prayers. A builder guarding with what he knew how to build. And third, notice the word still. The towers stand. Much of what stood round the pool in the misl years has been rebuilt or cleared, but these lookouts remain, and pilgrims walk past them on their way to the shrine. They no longer need watchmen in the old way. They've become a kind of sign: a sacred place is something people have chosen to guard. The Harmandir sits low, at the level of the water, with doors open on every side. In Sikh telling, those open doors are a welcome to all. And just beyond the edge of that openness, someone once built towers so the welcome could keep going. Guarding towers.

The Ramgarhia towers. The two lookouts of Jassa Singh Ramgarhia's bunga, built to guard the Harmandir, still standing near the sacred pool. Today's word.

903.title: When the misls quarreled
903.hook: as danger faded, rivalry grew between the misls
903.howItsDone: Sikh histories tell the misl rivalries frankly, and Sikhs read Guru Arjan's hymn on Ang 1299 of the Guru Granth Sahib about having no enemy and no stranger.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ramgarhia towers, plain brick lookouts built to guard the Harmandir. Your line was guarding towers. What precious thing did you stand guard over? Today, the story turns a little sour. Day nine hundred three.

A family pulls together beautifully at a funeral or in a hospital waiting room. Everyone brings food, nobody keeps score. Then the crisis passes, and months later two siblings aren't speaking over who got the good china. Sikh histories tell a story with the same shape. For a long time the misls were hunted, and they rode together because they had to. Then the hunters grew weaker, the misls held land, and the old enemy was no longer at the gate. Today: when the misls quarreled.
screen: `TOGETHER IN THE CRISIS.` → `APART WHEN IT PASSES.` → `THE MISLS HOLD THE LAND.`

segments.voice: Here's how Sikh histories describe the turn. While the danger was great, the bands needed one another. They met as the Sarbat Khalsa, agreed a gurmata, and rode under shared leaders. But once the misls held territory, each chief had something to lose, and something to gain at a neighbor's expense. Border villages. River crossings. Revenue. Marriages that tied one house to another, or failed to. The quarrels were not about faith. The chiefs bowed at the same Harmandir and heard the same scripture. They were about land and pride and who would lead. One story shows it. Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, the builder of yesterday's towers, was, Sikh histories say, pushed out of his lands for a time by rival chiefs, men who had once ridden beside him, and he lived beyond the Sutlej until he could come back. Other misls fought and made peace and fought again. The gatherings at Amritsar grew harder to hold together. Now set that beside the scripture they shared. In a hymn of Guru Arjan in the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang 1299, the singer says, in paraphrase, that no one is his enemy and no one a stranger; he has come to get along with everyone. The chiefs heard the same scripture at the same Harmandir. Hearing it didn't stop the quarrels. That's the honest part of this story, and it's the part worth keeping. Unity under pressure is real. But it's easier than unity at ease. When the shared danger lifts, the old grudges find room. Danger gone, rivalry grew.
screen: `THE DANGER LIFTED.` · `LAND, PRIDE AND WHO WOULD LEAD.` · `RAMGARHIA PUSHED ACROSS THE SUTLEJ.` · `NO ONE IS MY ENEMY.` · then, large: `DANGER GONE, RIVALRY GREW.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with one rivalry. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you've drifted into competing with, or quietly resenting: a sibling, a coworker, an old friend, another parent at the school gate. Remember a time you were on the same side. Then ask what the rivalry is really about. It may be small. Land, pride, who leads. Choose one small move that would cool it: a compliment, a message, letting them win one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

When the misls quarreled. Once the danger faded, the misls fought over land and leadership, even while sharing one scripture. This week: the Karorsinghia, the Shaheedan, the Phulkian states, twice a year at Amritsar, the bungas, the Ramgarhia towers, and the quarrels. Today's word.
Your line: danger gone, rivalry grew. Today, heal one rivalry, even a little. Send the message, give the compliment, or let them have this one. Day nine hundred three.
